topic.title: Velocity/time graphs (including two-journey problems)
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks, six questions, sat every Summer. This topic has twice been the long closing question: Summer 2022 Q4 (V from a deceleration 2, distance from areas 4, total time 4) and Summer 2023 Q6 (sketch 2, catch-up time 5, distance 2, which is ahead and by how far 5). Expect 8 to 14 marks over three to five parts, with the early marks for areas and gradients and the last marks for a formed equation and for reading which clock the question uses.
mustMemorise: Gradient of a velocity/time graph = acceleration; area under it = distance
Split the area into triangles, rectangles and trapezia at every joint
Area of a trapezium = half the sum of the parallel velocities, times the time
For a catch-up, write both distances as expressions in one time, equate and solve
Take off any head start before writing the answer, and add elapsed time back for a total
One constant-acceleration formula covers one stage, never a whole journey whose acceleration changes
notOnThisSpec: Curved velocity/time graphs, and tangents or areas estimated under them — Unit 2 uses straight sections only
Negative velocity on a velocity/time graph: the Teacher Guidance says these graphs have positive velocity only
Calculus: the area is never found by integrating and the gradient is never found by differentiating

mustBeAbleTo: Read an acceleration or a deceleration as the gradient of one section, using that section's own rise and run
Find a distance as an area, splitting the shape into triangles, rectangles and trapezia at every joint
Use the trapezium formula on a whole graph where the shape allows it, and use the split as a check
Sketch a velocity/time graph from a written description, including a stationary start
Form and solve an equation for an unknown stage time from the distance still to be covered
Write both vehicles' distances as expressions in one time, equate them and solve a catch-up problem
Convert between a time measured from one vehicle and a time measured from the other
Find an average speed from a velocity/time graph
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. This is the long question. Summer 2022 Q4 was 2 + 4 + 4: find V from a deceleration, find the distance in the first stages from areas, then the total time for a set distance. Summer 2023 Q6 was 2 + 5 + 2 + 5: sketch the second journey, find the catch-up time, find the distance, then decide which vehicle is ahead and by how far. Schemes are written in MW and W, with a mark for each correct area or expression and follow-through applied throughout.
traps: Taking the whole area as one rectangle at the greatest velocity (Summer 2022 Q4)
Leaving the one half out of a triangle or trapezium (Summer 2023 Q6(iii))
Giving the gradient where the area was asked for, or the area where the gradient was asked for
Stretching one constant-acceleration formula across a whole multi-stage journey (Summer 2022 Q4(iii))
Finding the last stage's time and handing that in as the total time (Summer 2022 Q4(iii))
Ignoring the head start, so the answer is on the wrong vehicle's clock (Summer 2023 Q6(ii))
Using a section's end time as its width instead of subtracting its start time (Summer 2023 Q6(i))
Quoting a deceleration as a negative number where the question asked for the deceleration itself
Summer 2024 Unit 2 Question 1. An average speed taken from a journey the candidates had just drawn was surprisingly poorly answered: only the stronger ones used total distance divided by total time.

steps.decision: The gradient of a velocity/time graph is the acceleration, because the rise is a change in velocity and the run is the time it took. Metres per second, per second.

options: Because the gradient of a velocity/time graph is the acceleration
Because the gradient of a velocity/time graph is the distance
Because the gradient of a velocity/time graph is the velocity
whyMenu.explain: Height is velocity, gradient is acceleration, area is distance. Those three readings are the whole topic, and mixing the last two is the commonest loss on it.

steps.decision: Distance is the area under the graph. Split the shape at every joint first: here a triangle while the train speeds up, a rectangle at steady speed, a triangle while it slows.
The middle stage lasts 50 - 20 = 30 s at a steady 24 m/s, so its area is a plain rectangle.
The last stage runs from 50 s to 80 s, so its base is 30 s and its height is the 24 m/s the train is losing.
Add the three pieces. The whole shape is a trapezium, so $\tfrac{1}{2}(80 + 30) \times 24$ gives the same $1320$ m in one line: use whichever you can see faster, and use the other to check.

workedExamples.stem:
A tram is travelling at 18 m/s along a straight track when it begins to brake, 600 m from its terminus.
It decelerates uniformly at 0.6 m/s² for 10 seconds, reaching a velocity of $V$ m/s.
It then travels at $V$ m/s for 25 seconds.
Finally it decelerates uniformly, coming to rest exactly at the terminus.

(i) Calculate the value of $V$.
(ii) Calculate how far the tram travels in the first 35 seconds.
(iii) Calculate the whole time the tram takes to cover the 600 m.

steps.decision: Deceleration means the velocity is falling, so subtract. Reading the gradient off the graph gives the same thing: a drop of 0.6 m/s in every second for 10 seconds.
That stage is a trapezium: parallel sides 18 m/s and 12 m/s, width 10 s. Half the sum of the parallel sides, times the width.

steps.working: Steady stage: $12 \times 25 = 300$ m, so the first 35 s cover $150 + 300 = 450$ m
steps.decision: A rectangle this time. The two stages together are the 10 + 25 seconds the part asks about.
This is the step that makes the last part possible. The tram has 600 m in total, so whatever is left after the first two stages must be covered by the final triangle.
The last stage is a triangle of height 12 m/s and unknown base $t$. Writing its area and setting it equal to the distance left turns the geometry into an equation with one unknown.
The question asks for the whole journey, so add the 35 seconds already gone to the 25 seconds just found. Handing in the 25 on its own is the loss the examiners reported in Summer 2022.

twin.stem: A tram travelling at 20 m/s decelerates uniformly at 0.5 m/s² for 8 seconds. Calculate its velocity at the end of the 8 seconds.

workedExamples.stem:
A bus passes a stationary taxi at a constant 12 m/s and keeps that velocity.
8 seconds later the taxi sets off, accelerating uniformly for 12 seconds to reach 20 m/s, and then holds 20 m/s until it draws level with the bus.

(i) Calculate the time, measured from the moment the taxi starts moving, until it draws level with the bus.
(ii) Calculate the distance the taxi has travelled in that time.

figure.alt: A velocity/time graph with two journeys: the bus as a horizontal line at 12 m/s, and the taxi at rest until 8 s, rising in a straight line to 20 m/s, reaching that speed after 20 seconds, then horizontal, with a dashed line at 35 s where the areas are equal.

steps.working: Let $T$ be the time measured from the moment the bus passed the taxi.
steps.decision: One clock for both vehicles. Starting the taxi's clock at zero is what wrecks this question: every distance then refers to a different moment.
The bus keeps a steady velocity, so its area is a rectangle of height 12 and width $T$.

steps.working: Taxi, first 12 s of motion: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 20 = 120$ m
steps.decision: The taxi's graph is a triangle while it speeds up. It reaches 20 m/s at $T = 8 + 12 = 20$ s on the shared clock.

steps.working: Taxi, after that: $20(T - 20)$, so the taxi has gone $120 + 20(T - 20)$
steps.decision: A rectangle whose width is however long the taxi has been at full speed. Both distances are now expressions in the same $T$, which is exactly what the examiners said the successful candidates wrote down.
Level means equal distances from the same starting line, so set the two expressions equal and solve. The equation is linear, so no formula is needed.

steps.working: Time after the taxi starts $= 35 - 8 = 27$ s
steps.decision: Read the question again. $T$ is measured from the bus passing, and the part asks for the time from when the taxi started, so take off the 8-second head start.
The two vehicles are level, so either expression gives the distance. The bus's rectangle is the quicker one, and the taxi's areas can be used to check it.

twin.stem: A cyclist travelling at a constant 9 m/s passes a stationary scooter. 5 seconds later the scooter sets off, accelerating uniformly for 10 seconds to 18 m/s and then holding that velocity. Calculate the time, measured from the moment the cyclist passed, until the scooter draws level.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a triangle has base 12 and height 9. What is its area?

options.feedback: Half the base times the height: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 9 = 54$.
That is the rectangle around the triangle. The one half is missing.
That adds the base and the height. Area multiplies them.
That divides the two lengths, which gives a ratio rather than an area.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a trapezium has parallel sides 6 and 10 and a width of 8 between them. What is its area?

options.feedback: Half the sum of the parallel sides, times the width: $\tfrac{1}{2}(6 + 10) \times 8 = 64$.
The one half has been left out, so the answer is exactly twice the area.
That is a rectangle at the longer side. A trapezium uses the average of the two parallel sides.
That is a rectangle at the shorter side, which is too small.

items.skill: Prerequisite: gradient of a straight line
items.stem: From an earlier topic: a straight line runs from $(0, 0)$ to $(8, 16)$. What is its gradient?

options.feedback: Rise 16 over run 8 gives 2.
The fraction is upside down: that is run over rise.
That multiplies the two, which gives an area rather than a gradient.
That is the run on its own. Divide the rise by it.

items.skill: Prerequisite: solve a linear equation with a bracket

options.feedback: Expanding gives $8x = 12x - 60$, so $4x = 60$ and $x = 15$.
The $+60$ has been dropped: that leaves $8x = 12x - 120$, so $4x = 120$ and $x = 30$. Keep the 60, and expanding gives $8x = 12x - 60$.
A sign has slipped when the $12x$ crossed the equals sign. Take $8x$ from both sides, not the other way round.
That comes from $20x = 60$, which adds the two $x$ terms instead of subtracting.

items.skill: Name what the gradient of a velocity/time graph gives
items.stem: What does the gradient of a velocity/time graph give?

options.feedback: Change in velocity divided by time: metres per second, per second.
Distance is the area underneath, not the slope. Mixing these two is the commonest loss on this topic.
Velocity is the height of the graph. The slope says how fast that height is changing.
Displacement, like distance, comes from the area under the graph.

items.skill: Name what the area under a velocity/time graph gives
items.stem: What does the area between a velocity/time graph and the time axis give?

options.feedback: Velocity multiplied by time is a distance, and that is exactly what an area on these axes measures.
Acceleration is the gradient. The area has units of metres per second times seconds, which is metres.
The area gives the distance. Dividing it by the total time would then give the average speed.
The final velocity is the height of the graph at the end, which is a reading rather than an area.

items.skill: Read a horizontal section on velocity/time axes
items.stem: A velocity/time graph is horizontal at 14 m/s for 20 seconds. What is happening?

options.text: The body keeps a steady 14 m/s and covers 280 m
options.feedback: Flat means the velocity is not changing, so the acceleration is zero. The area is the rectangle 14 x 20.

options.text: The body is at rest for 20 seconds
options.feedback: That is what a flat section means on displacement/time axes. Here the height is the velocity, and 14 m/s is not rest.

options.text: The body covers no distance, because the graph is flat
options.feedback: The graph is flat but the area underneath is not zero: the rectangle is 280 m tall by wide.
Steady acceleration would be a sloping straight line. A horizontal line has gradient zero, so the acceleration is zero.

items.skill: Read a falling section as a deceleration
items.stem: A velocity/time graph falls in a straight line from 24 m/s to rest in 8 seconds. What is the deceleration?

options.feedback: The gradient is -3 m/s², and a deceleration of 3 m/s² is the same statement said the other way round.

options.text: -3 m/s², because deceleration is always negative
options.feedback: The gradient is -3. A question that asks for the deceleration wants its size, so write 3 m/s² and say it is a deceleration.
24 x 8 is an area, which would be a distance if the graph were a rectangle. An acceleration is a gradient: divide instead.
That is the run divided by the rise. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time, so 24 divided by 8.

items.skill: Choose the right area formula for a sloping stage
items.stem: On a velocity/time graph a straight section rises from 8 m/s to 20 m/s over 15 seconds. Which calculation gives the distance covered in that section?

options.feedback: A trapezium: half the sum of the two parallel sides, times the width. That is 210 m.
That treats the section as a rectangle at the highest velocity, which counts the empty triangle above the line as distance travelled.
The one half has gone. That doubles the trapezium, giving 420 m instead of 210 m.
That is the gradient, so it gives the acceleration in m/s². The distance is an area.

items.skill: Handle a head start in a catch-up problem
items.stem: A van passes a parked car at a steady velocity. 6 seconds later the car sets off. Working with one clock that starts when the van passes, you find the car draws level at $T = 33$ s. The question asks for the time from the moment the car started. What do you write?

options.feedback: The car's own clock started 6 seconds later, so take the head start off: 33 - 6 = 27 s.
That is the time on the shared clock, measured from the van passing. The Summer 2023 examiners reported this exact step as the one candidates missed.
The head start is taken off, not added: the car has been moving for less time than the van, not more.
That is the head start on its own. It is the correction, not the answer.

items.skill: Refuse one formula across a whole multi-stage journey
items.stem: A car speeds up from rest for 8 s to reach 30 m/s, holds 30 m/s for 12 s, then brakes to rest, covering 700 m in all. A student writes $700 = \tfrac{1}{2}(30 + 0)t$ for the whole journey. What is wrong with that?

options.text: The acceleration is not the same throughout, so one constant-acceleration formula cannot cover the whole journey
options.feedback: Constant-acceleration formulae apply to one stage at a time. Across the three stages, use the area under the graph.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the arithmetic is right
options.feedback: The formula assumes one steady acceleration from start to finish, and this journey has three different ones. The Summer 2022 examiners saw this attempted across a whole journey and it earned nothing.
The distance is not the problem: the formula is being applied to a journey whose acceleration changes twice.

options.text: The formula should have been $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$
options.feedback: Swapping to another constant-acceleration formula does not help: every one of them assumes a single steady acceleration.

options.feedback: Change in velocity over change in time, which is what an acceleration is.

The height is the velocity at that moment.

options.text: The length of the time axis
options.feedback: That is just how long the journey lasted.

parts.stem: On a velocity/time graph, which reading gives the distance travelled?

options.text: The area between the graph and the time axis
options.feedback: Velocity times time is a distance, and that product is what an area measures here.
The gradient is the acceleration, in m/s².
That is the greatest velocity, a single reading rather than a total.

options.text: The greatest height times the total time
options.feedback: That would be right only if the graph were a rectangle all the way across.

hints: What are the units of height times width on these axes?
parts.workedSolution: Metres per second, multiplied by seconds, gives metres. The area under the graph is the distance travelled.

parts.stem: A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 18 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.
hints: Change in velocity divided by the time it took.
parts.workedSolution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{18 - 0}{6} = 3$ m/s².

parts.stem: A body decelerates uniformly from 24 m/s to rest in 8 seconds. Calculate its deceleration.
hints: The velocity falls by the same amount every second.
A deceleration is quoted as a positive size.
parts.workedSolution: The gradient is $\dfrac{0 - 24}{8} = -3$ m/s², so the deceleration is $3$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right and the division $24 \div 8$ earns the method mark (M). The part asks for the deceleration, which is quoted as a positive size, so write 3 m/s² and say it is a deceleration.
That multiplies the velocity by the time, which gives an area and so a distance in metres. An acceleration is a gradient, so divide.
The fraction is upside down. Acceleration is the change in velocity on top and the time underneath.

parts.stem: A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels in those 10 seconds.
hints: Sketch the graph: it is a triangle.
Area of a triangle is half the base times the height.
parts.workedSolution: The graph is a triangle with base $10$ s and height $15$ m/s, so the distance is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 15 = 75$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The one half has been left out, so this is the rectangle around the triangle. The method mark (M) for using the area is safe; the working mark (W) needs the halving.

parts.stem: A body travels at a constant 12 m/s for 25 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels.
hints: The graph is a rectangle.
parts.workedSolution: The area is a rectangle: $12 \times 25 = 300$ m.

parts.stem: A body's velocity rises uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s over 15 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels in those 15 seconds.
hints: The shape is a trapezium with parallel sides 8 and 20.
Half the sum of the parallel sides, times the width.
parts.workedSolution: Distance $= \tfrac{1}{2}(8 + 20) \times 15 = 210$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rectangle at the highest velocity, which counts the empty triangle above the line as distance covered. The body only reaches 20 m/s at the end.
The sum of the parallel sides is right, which is worth the method mark (M). It is half that sum that multiplies the width, so the working mark (W) needs the answer halved.

parts.stem: The graph shows the velocity of a bus on a straight road. Calculate the total distance travelled by the bus in the 55 seconds.

scheme.for: any one correct area from the three stages

hints: Split the shape at each joint: triangle, rectangle, triangle.
Or treat the whole shape as one trapezium.
parts.workedSolution: Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 15 = 75$ m; rectangle $30 \times 15 = 450$ m; triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 15 = 112.5$ m. Total $= 637.5$ m. As one trapezium: $\tfrac{1}{2}(55 + 30) \times 15 = 637.5$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole rectangle from 0 to 55 seconds at 15 m/s. The bus is below 15 m/s while it speeds up and while it slows, so those two triangles have to come off.
The parallel sides of 55 s and 30 s and the height of 15 m/s are all right, which is worth the method mark (M). The trapezium formula halves that sum, so the working mark (W) needs the answer halved.
The rectangle in the middle is right, and that alone earns a method mark (M). The two triangles at either end are part of the journey as well.

parts.stem: Use the graph to calculate how far the bus travels between $t = 10$ s and $t = 40$ s.
hints: Between those times the graph is horizontal.
The width of the rectangle is 40 - 10.
parts.workedSolution: Between $t = 10$ and $t = 40$ the velocity is a steady $15$ m/s for $30$ s, so the distance is $15 \times 30 = 450$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The height of 15 m/s is right, so the method mark (M) stands. The width is the 30 s this stage lasts, found by taking 10 from 40, not the clock reading of 40 s.

parts.stem: Calculate the deceleration of the bus during the last stage of its journey.

scheme.for: 15 divided by 15, from the last stage

hints: The last stage runs from 40 s to 55 s.
The velocity falls from 15 m/s to 0.
parts.workedSolution: The gradient is $\dfrac{0 - 15}{55 - 40} = -1$ m/s², so the deceleration is $1$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right and the division $15 \div 15$ earns the method mark (M). The part asks for the deceleration, which is quoted as a positive size, so write 1 m/s² and say it is a deceleration.
The drop of 15 m/s is right, which earns the method mark (M). Divide it by the 15 s the braking stage lasted rather than by the 55 s of the whole journey.

context.setting: Forming an equation for an unknown time

parts.stem: A body decelerates uniformly from 16 m/s to rest, covering 128 m as it does so. Calculate the time it takes to stop.

scheme.for: an area written as half of 16 times t

hints: Sketch the graph: a triangle of height 16 m/s and unknown base.
Its area is the 128 m covered.
parts.workedSolution: The graph is a triangle of height $16$ m/s and base $t$, so $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times t = 128$. That gives $8t = 128$, so $t = 16$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: Writing $16t = 128$ leaves the one half out, so the triangle has been treated as a rectangle. With the half in place the equation reads $8t = 128$.

context.setting: A catch-up with a head start

parts.stem:
A cyclist travelling at a constant 10 m/s passes a stationary scooter. 4 seconds later the scooter sets off, accelerating uniformly for 10 seconds to reach 20 m/s, and then holds 20 m/s.

Calculate the time, measured from the moment the cyclist passed, until the scooter draws level with her.
hints: Use one clock, starting when the cyclist passes.
The scooter's triangle is half of 10 times 20.
It reaches 20 m/s at T = 4 + 10 = 14 s.
parts.workedSolution:
Let $T$ be the time from the moment the cyclist passed.
Cyclist: $10T$.
Scooter: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m while it accelerates, then $20(T - 14)$.
Equating: $10T = 100 + 20T - 280$, so $10T = 180$ and $T = 18$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the time from the moment the scooter started. This part measures from when the cyclist passed, so the 4-second head start belongs in the answer rather than taken off it.

parts.stem:
A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 6 seconds, then travels at a constant 12 m/s for a further 10 seconds.

On the grid, draw the velocity/time graph for these 16 seconds.
hints: Mark the joints first: (0, 0), (6, 12) and (16, 12).
Both sections are straight lines.
parts.workedSolution: Two straight segments: up from $(0, 0)$ to $(6, 12)$, then horizontal from $(6, 12)$ to $(16, 12)$.

pattern.test: the flat section stopped at the stage's own length: point plotted at (10, 12)

commonErrors.feedback: The 10 seconds are a further 10 seconds, so they are counted on from 6 s and the flat section ends at $6 + 10 = 16$ s. Stopping at $t = 10$ reads the stage's own length as a clock reading.

context.setting: Average speed from a velocity/time graph

parts.stem: A body accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 seconds and then decelerates uniformly to rest in a further 30 seconds. Calculate its average speed over the 40 seconds.

scheme.for: the area as half of 40 times 20

hints: The graph is one triangle of base 40 s and height 20 m/s.
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.
parts.workedSolution: The whole graph is a triangle: distance $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 20 = 400$ m. Average speed $= \dfrac{400}{40} = 10$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the distance travelled, which is the area. Average speed divides that distance by the 40 s the journey took.

That treats the whole graph as a rectangle at 20 m/s, which gives a distance rather than a speed and counts the empty space above the two sloping lines. The area is the triangle, 400 m, and the average speed divides it by 40 s.

parts.stem: In which stage of the bus's journey is the size of the acceleration greatest?

options.text: The first stage, from 0 to 10 s
options.feedback: The gradients are 1.5 m/s², 0 and -1 m/s². Taking sizes, 1.5 is the largest, and it is the steepest line on the picture.

options.text: The last stage, from 40 to 55 s
options.feedback: That stage has a gradient of -1 m/s², which is less steep than the first stage's 1.5 m/s².

options.text: The middle stage, from 10 to 40 s
options.feedback: The middle stage is horizontal, so its acceleration is zero. It is the longest stage, not the steepest.

options.text: The last stage, because it covers more ground than the first
options.feedback: How much ground a stage covers is its area, which says nothing about how steep it is.

hints: Acceleration is steepness, so compare the slopes and ignore their signs.
parts.workedSolution: The three gradients are $1.5$, $0$ and $-1$ m/s². The steepest is the first stage.

figures.alt: A velocity/time graph for a lorry: a straight line from (0, 0) to (8, 16), a horizontal line to (30, 16), then a straight line down to (40, 0), with the area beneath shaded.

parts.stem:
The velocity/time graph shows a lorry pulling away from a junction on a straight road.

Calculate the acceleration of the lorry during the first 8 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: Gradient of the first section.
The velocity rises from 0 to 16 m/s.
parts.workedSolution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{16}{8} = 2$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rectangle 16 by 8, an area rather than a gradient. Acceleration divides the change in velocity by the time.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total distance travelled by the lorry in the 40 seconds.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: any one of the three areas correct

hints: Split the area at each joint, or use the trapezium in one line.
The parallel sides of the trapezium are 40 s and 22 s.
parts.workedSolution: Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 16 = 64$ m; rectangle $22 \times 16 = 352$ m; triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 16 = 80$ m. Total $= 496$ m, which is also $\tfrac{1}{2}(40 + 22) \times 16$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one rectangle across the whole 40 seconds at 16 m/s. The lorry is slower than that while it speeds up and while it brakes, so the two triangles have to come off.
The parallel sides of 40 s and 22 s and the height of 16 m/s are all right, so the method mark (M) is safe. The trapezium formula takes half their sum, so the working mark (W) needs the halving.

parts.stem:
Calculate the deceleration of the lorry during the last 10 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The velocity falls from 16 m/s to 0 in 10 s.
parts.workedSolution: The gradient is $\dfrac{0 - 16}{10} = -1.6$ m/s², so the deceleration is $1.6$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right and the division $16 \div 10$ earns the method mark (M). The part asks for the deceleration, which is quoted as a positive size, so write 1.6 m/s² and say it is a deceleration.
The drop of 16 m/s is right, so the method mark (M) stands. The braking lasted 10 s, from 30 s to 40 s, not the whole 40 s of the journey.

context.setting: A car braking on the approach to a level crossing

parts.stem:
A car is travelling at 30 m/s along a straight road when the driver sees a level crossing 700 m ahead.
She decelerates uniformly at 1.25 m/s² for 8 seconds, reaching a velocity of $V$ m/s.
She then travels at $V$ m/s for 12 seconds.
Finally she brakes uniformly, coming to rest exactly at the crossing.

Calculate the value of $V$.

Answer ________
hints: The velocity falls by 1.25 m/s in every second.
Over 8 seconds that is a fall of 10 m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The 1.25 has been added rather than taken off. The car is decelerating, so its velocity falls: 30 - 10, not 30 + 10.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance travelled by the car in the first 20 seconds.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: the braking stage as half of (30 + 20) times 8
the steady stage as 20 times 12, giving 240

hints: The first 20 seconds are the first two stages.
The first stage is a trapezium and the second a rectangle.
parts.workedSolution:
Braking stage: $\tfrac{1}{2}(30 + 20) \times 8 = 200$ m.
Steady stage: $20 \times 12 = 240$ m.
Total $= 200 + 240 = 440$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30 m/s held for the whole 20 seconds. The car is only at 30 m/s for an instant at the start, so the first stage is a trapezium and the second a rectangle at 20 m/s.
That is the first stage with the one half left out, and the second stage missing as well. The trapezium is half of (30 + 20) times 8, which is 200 m, and the rectangle of 240 m still has to be added.
The braking stage of 200 m is right and earns its method marks (M). The question asks for the first 20 seconds, so the 240 m of the steady stage belongs in the total.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total time taken by the car to travel the 700 m to the level crossing.

Answer ________ s

scheme.for: the last stage written as half of 20 times t

hints: Work out how much of the 700 m is still to run after the first 20 seconds.
The last stage is a triangle of height 20 m/s and unknown base.
The question asks for the total time, so the first 20 seconds are part of the answer.
parts.workedSolution:
Distance left $= 700 - 440 = 260$ m.
The last stage is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times t = 260$, so $t = 26$ s.
Total time $= 8 + 12 + 26 = 46$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the time for the last stage on its own, and it earns the method marks (M) that lead to it. The question asks for the whole 700 m, so add the 20 seconds already gone.

That stretches one constant-acceleration formula over the whole 700 m, as though the deceleration never changed. It changes twice, so work stage by stage from the area under the graph. The Summer 2022 examiners reported this attempt on the same kind of last part.

context.setting: A motorcyclist catching a van on a straight road

parts.stem:
A van travelling at a constant 16 m/s passes a motorcyclist who is waiting at the side of a straight road.
6 seconds later the motorcyclist sets off, accelerating uniformly for 10 seconds to reach 24 m/s. She then holds 24 m/s until she draws level with the van, which happens 33 seconds after the van first passed her.

On the grid, draw the velocity/time graph for the motorcyclist over those 33 seconds.

scheme.for: a horizontal line along the time axis to (6, 0), then a straight line to (16, 24)

hints: She is at rest for the first 6 seconds, so the graph runs along the time axis.
She reaches 24 m/s at t = 6 + 10 = 16 s.
After that the graph is horizontal.
parts.workedSolution: Along the time axis from $(0, 0)$ to $(6, 0)$; a straight line from $(6, 0)$ to $(16, 24)$; a horizontal line from $(16, 24)$ to $(33, 24)$.

pattern.test: drawn from a false origin at her own start: points plotted at (10, 24) and (27, 24)

commonErrors.feedback: The shape is right, and the drawing keeps both its marks: the Summer 2023 examiners accepted a false origin like this on the diagram. The warning is for what comes next. Every joint sits 6 s to the left because the graph starts at her own moment of setting off, and both vehicles share one clock, and a question that asks when they meet needs the same origin. On that shared clock her line runs along the axis until $t = 6$ s and reaches 24 m/s at $t = 16$ s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the time, measured from the moment the motorcyclist starts moving, until she draws level with the van.

Answer ________ s

scheme.for: the motorcyclist's accelerating distance as half of 10 times 24
the two distances equated and solved to give T = 33
27, after taking off the 6-second head start

hints: Use one clock, starting when the van passed.
Write both distances as expressions in that one time.
Read the question again before writing the answer: whose clock does it use?
parts.workedSolution:
Let $T$ be the time from the moment the van passed.
Van: $16T$.
Motorcyclist: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 24 = 120$ m up to $T = 16$ s, then $24(T - 16)$.
Equating: $16T = 120 + 24T - 384$, so $8T = 264$ and $T = 33$ s.
From the moment she started: $33 - 6 = 27$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: The equation has been solved correctly, so four of the five marks are already earned. That 33 s is measured from the moment the van passed; this part measures from when she started, so take off the 6-second head start.
The head start has been added rather than taken off. She has been moving for less time than the van, not more, so her own clock reads 33 - 6.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance the motorcyclist has travelled when she draws level with the van.

Answer ________ m
hints: Level means the two have covered the same distance from the same point.
The van's rectangle is the quicker one to work out.
parts.workedSolution: They are level, so her distance equals the van's: $16 \times 33 = 528$ m. Checking with her own areas: $120 + 24 \times 17 = 528$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses her 27 seconds with the van's velocity. The van has been travelling for the full 33 seconds, and it is the van's 33 seconds that measure the distance they have both covered.

parts.stem:
The moment she draws level, the motorcyclist decelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² until she comes to rest. The van keeps its velocity of 16 m/s.

Calculate how far ahead of the motorcyclist the van is at the moment she comes to rest.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: her time to stop as 24 divided by 2, giving 12
her distance as half of 12 times 24, giving 144
the van's distance as 16 times 12, giving 192

hints: Find how long she takes to stop first.
Her graph over that time is a triangle; the van's is a rectangle.
Both start from the same place, so subtract the two distances.
parts.workedSolution:
Time to stop $= \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ s.
Her distance $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 24 = 144$ m.
The van's distance $= 16 \times 12 = 192$ m.
Gap $= 192 - 144 = 48$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is her triangle with the one half missing, handed in as the gap. With the half it is 144 m, and the gap is the van's 192 m minus that.
Her own stopping distance of 144 m is right and earns its method marks (M). The question asks how far ahead the van is, so take that 144 m from the van's 192 m.

figures.alt: A velocity/time graph for a ferry: a straight line from (0, 0) to (30, 9), a horizontal line to (90, 9), a straight line down to (120, 3), then a horizontal line to (160, 3), with the area beneath shaded.

parts.stem:
The velocity/time graph shows a ferry leaving a berth along a straight approach.

Calculate the acceleration of the ferry during the first 30 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: The velocity rises from 0 to 9 m/s in 30 s.
parts.workedSolution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{9}{30} = 0.3$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: The fraction is upside down, so this is seconds per metre per second. Acceleration puts the change in velocity on top.

parts.stem:
Calculate the distance travelled by the ferry between $t = 90$ s and $t = 120$ s.

Answer ________ m
hints: That stage is a trapezium with parallel sides 9 and 3.
Its width is 120 - 90.
parts.workedSolution: Distance $= \tfrac{1}{2}(9 + 3) \times 30 = 180$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The parallel sides and the width are right, so the method mark (M) is safe. The trapezium takes half their sum, so the working mark (W) needs the answer halved.
That is a rectangle at 9 m/s, but the ferry is slowing throughout this stage and finishes at 3 m/s. The shape is a trapezium.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total distance travelled by the ferry in the 160 seconds.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: any two of the four areas correct

hints: Four stages, four areas: triangle, rectangle, trapezium, rectangle.
You already have the third one.
parts.workedSolution: Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 9 = 135$ m; rectangle $60 \times 9 = 540$ m; trapezium $180$ m; rectangle $40 \times 3 = 120$ m. Total $= 975$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one rectangle at 9 m/s across the whole 160 seconds. The ferry is below 9 m/s for the first 30 seconds and for the last 70, so those parts of the rectangle are not distance travelled.
The first two stages give 675 m and earn their method marks (M). The graph carries on past 90 seconds, so the trapezium and the last rectangle belong in the total as well.

parts.stem:
Calculate the average speed of the ferry over the 160 seconds. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.
The total distance is the area you have just found.
parts.workedSolution: Average speed $= \dfrac{975}{160} = 6.09375$, which is $6.09$ m/s correct to 2 decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mean of the two steady velocities on the graph. Average speed divides the whole distance by the whole time, so it is 975 over 160.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairí is finding the total distance the train travels. Its velocity/time graph rises from rest to 24 m/s in 20 s, stays at 24 m/s until 50 s, then falls to rest at 80 s. His working:
studentWorking: The graph goes up to 24 m/s and lasts 80 s
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 treats the whole area as one rectangle, 24 m/s tall and 80 s wide. The train is only at 24 m/s between 20 s and 50 s: for the first 20 seconds and the last 30 it is slower than that, so the two triangles above the graph are counted as distance the train never travelled.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line is the right idea and it earns the method mark (M): distance really is the area under the graph. The working mark (W) needs the shape split at every joint, or the whole thing treated as one trapezium: half of (80 + 30) times 24 gives the same 1320 m in a single line.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is finding how long the taxi takes to catch the bus. The bus passes the stationary taxi at 12 m/s. 8 s later the taxi sets off, accelerating uniformly for 12 s to 20 m/s and then holding that velocity. The question asks for the time from the moment the taxi starts moving. Her working:
studentWorking: Let T be the time from when the bus passed
T = 35 s, so the answer is 35 s
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line up to the solution is right, and $T = 35$ s is the correct value of $T$. But $T$ was defined in line 1 as the time from the moment the bus passed, and the question asks for the time from the moment the taxi started. The taxi began 8 seconds later, so it has been moving for 8 seconds less.
correction: T = 35 s, measured from the moment the bus passed
Time from the moment the taxi started = 35 − 8 = 27 s
findTheMistake.feedback: This is a strong solution that loses its last mark in the final line. Four method marks (M) are safely earned, because the two distance expressions and the equation are exactly what the scheme rewards. The working mark (W) is for reading back which clock the question uses. The Summer 2023 examiners reported this same step — reaching the right time and then not dealing with the head start — as the one that separated the answers.

findTheMistake.stem: Séamus is finding the distance a ferry covers while its velocity falls uniformly from 9 m/s to 3 m/s over 30 seconds. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The shape and its measurements are both right. Line 3 leaves out the one half, so the answer is exactly twice the area: the formula is $\tfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h$, not $(a + b)h$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the trapezium and reading its three measurements off the graph is the method mark (M), and it is safely earned here. The working mark (W) goes with the halving. A quick check that catches this every time: the answer must lie between the rectangle at 3 m/s, which is 90 m, and the rectangle at 9 m/s, which is 270 m.

prompts.prompt: What does the gradient of a velocity/time graph give?
prompts.answer: The acceleration: the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

prompts.prompt: What does the area under a velocity/time graph give?
prompts.answer: The distance travelled. Metres per second times seconds gives metres.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the distance from a multi-stage velocity/time graph?
prompts.answer: Split the area at every joint into triangles, rectangles and trapezia, work out each one, and add them. Or treat the whole shape as a single trapezium where it is one.

prompts.prompt: Write the area of a trapezium under a velocity/time graph.
prompts.answer: Half the sum of the two parallel velocities, multiplied by the time the stage lasts.

prompts.prompt: Why is the greatest velocity times the total time usually wrong for the distance?
prompts.answer: Because it counts the empty space above the sloping parts as distance travelled. It is only right when the graph is one rectangle all the way across.

prompts.prompt: How do you handle a catch-up question on a velocity/time graph?
prompts.answer: Use one clock for both bodies, write each distance as an expression in that single time, set the two expressions equal and solve.

prompts.prompt: You solve a catch-up problem and get T = 33 s. What must you check before writing it down?
prompts.answer: Which clock the question uses. If T was measured from the first vehicle and the question asks about the second, take off the head start.

prompts.prompt: A journey finishes with a braking stage whose time is unknown. How do you find it?
prompts.answer: Work out the distance left to run, write the area of that last stage in terms of the unknown time, set the two equal and solve.

prompts.prompt: Can one constant-acceleration formula be used across a whole multi-stage journey?
prompts.answer: No. Each formula assumes a single steady acceleration, so it applies to one stage at a time. Across stages, use the area under the graph.

prompts.prompt: How do you get an average speed from a velocity/time graph?
prompts.answer: Find the total distance as the area under the graph, then divide by the total time.

findings.asked: Velocity-time graph: distance from areas, then a time for a final stage.
findings.wentWrong: Areas under segments earned marks widely; the final time was attempted with one constant-acceleration formula over the whole journey; the 18 s already elapsed was forgotten.
findings.rule: Distance = area under the graph, segment by segment.

findings.asked: Draw a second journey on a velocity-time graph; find when one catches the other.
findings.wentWrong: A false origin of 10 s was accepted on the graph but then mishandled in the algebra; the 10 s head start was ignored; equations of motion were tried unsuccessfully instead of two distance expressions in T.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the two distances as expressions in T (areas), equated them, and solved.
findings.rule: Equal distances at the catch-up time - write both areas in terms of T.

findings.asked: Draw a displacement-time graph and find an average speed.
findings.wentWrong: Weaker candidates could not draw the graph (extra parts, wrong heights); the average speed - a GCSE Maths skill - was poorly done: only the stronger used total distance over total time.
findings.rule: Average speed = total distance / total time.

insight.ruleToRemember: Area under a velocity-time graph is distance; equate distance expressions in T for catch-up problems and account for any head start; average speed is total distance over total time.
